title: IDX VL-PD1 USB-C V-Mount Charger First Look at Inter BEE 2026 - Newsshooter
content: At Inter BEE 2026 in Japan, IDX was showcasing its new VL-PD1 USB-C V-Mount Charger, which allows you to charge a V-mount battery (regardless of whether it features a USB-C input or not) via USB-C PD. It looks to be an interesting solution for anyone who travels a lot or needs to reduce space. If you own or use batteries that don’t have a USB-C input, it’s a good alternative to having to carry around large and bulky V-mount chargers. The VL-PD1 is very lightweight (300g / 10.58 oz), and it accepts a USB Type-C PD input (minimum 20W, up to 100W). When paired with a 75W or higher PD power source (such as IDX’s UC-PD series), it delivers up to 4A / 16.8V for fast charging. You can use a lower wattage source, but the charging time will increase. If you use select IDX batteries that can communicate with the VL-PD1, the plate has built-in Bluetooth, so you can use a free IDX app to monitor the charging status and battery health. The IDX mobile app can monitor up to eight VL-PD1 plates simultaneously. For mounting, it features four M3 mounting holes for installing flat on a shelf, inside a DIT cart, or upright on a wall/19-inch rack. I would have liked to have seen a version with a plate on both sides, so you could charge two batteries at once, either through two separate USB-C PD power sources or through just one. The IDX VL-PD1 USB-C V-Mount Charger is currently only available in Japan, but it will be coming to overseas markets soon; no official pricing is available. title: DOWN release ‘Volume V,’ share new video - NextMosh

Share the post "DOWN release ‘Volume V’ album, share animated video for “They Walk The Night”" DOWN have released their new studio album, Volume V, today (November 20) through Nuclear Blast Records, alongside an animated music video for the track “They Walk The Night.”Stream Albums The video was created by Freakshot Films and follows the previously released clips for “Blood Oath” and “The Myth.” Volume V marks the New Orleans metal band’s first full-length album since 2007’s Down III: Over The Under, following the release of two EPs in 2012 and 2014.Stream Heavy Metal “It’s an instant classic for DOWN folks,” guitarist Pepper Keenan said of the new song. Drummer Jimmy Bower added, “It’s my favorite song of the album! It’s got DOWN/Trouble vibes!” The 10-track album was developed during writing sessions at vocalist Philip H. Anselmo’s home studio, Nodferatu’s Lair, with much of the material taking shape throughout 2025. Guitarists Keenan and Kirk Windstein recorded their parts simultaneously during the sessions. The band’s current lineup consists of Anselmo on vocals, Keenan and Windstein on guitars, Bower on drums and Pat Bruders on bass.Stream Albums DOWN will celebrate the album’s release with a performance tonight (November 20) at The Great NOLA Trendkill at Lakefront Arena in New Orleans. The two-day festival also features Pantera, Black Label Society, Corrosion Of Conformity, Power Trip, Crowbar, Eyehategod and others. The band will also headline the second day of Decibel Magazine Metal & Beer Fest Denver on December 5, marking their first appearance in the city in more than 12 years. Volume V is available now on CD, vinyl and digital platforms.

HOWE, Texas (KTEN) — Friday night football can mean so much more than what happens on the field across countless small Texas towns. In Howe, one light has come to represent generations of football. It's generations of Bulldogs... families in the stands... and a fanbase that knows when there's something to celebrate. For decades, that celebration has had a guiding light. “That's how I knew that the Bulldogs won on Friday night," said Howe play-by-play announcer Monte Walker. The victory “V” first lit up in 1977, introduced as a way for townspeople to know when their Bulldogs had won. "When i was a kid, it was kind of the internet,” Walker said. “If I didn't get to go to the game on Friday night, I'd ride my bike across town to see if the victory light was lit on Saturday morning." The Howe Bulldogs victory “V” at its former location at the football stadium. That boy would eventually wear the Howe uniform himself... and get to experience the tradition from the other side. After the 1991 season, the original “V” was replaced. And the tradition that meant so much to the Bulldog faithful began to fade. "About 2008, I contacted Superintendent Kevin Wilson at the time and said, ‘Hey, we really need to get this tradition back. There's a lot of people that want to reignite this thing,’" Walker recalled. In 2008, the “V” was re-established, and it’s been shining ever since. While the signal has moved from the stadium to downtown, its meaning hasn't changed. "The community — win, lose or draw — they really do love their Bulldogs,” said head coach Jake Smith. “And they're going to be behind you no matter what." When Smith arrived in Howe, he quickly learned this wasn't just another postgame tradition; it was something that united his players and the people who make the city tick, around the Bulldogs’ success. “And it's always kind of like … bragging rights,” Smith said. “It’s fun listening to those kids who want to do something, and they have something to play for. " Because in a small town like Howe, the connection to football doesn't end when the players leave the field. It lives on through the families... the former players... and the next generation of Bulldogs. "I hope there's an eight-year-old out there right now who is just like I was,” Walker said. “You know, riding their bike maybe to see if that victory light's on downtown." In Howe, a victory “V” is more than a sign of a win… it's a reminder that Bulldog pride never really goes dark. title: The Chelsea Lineup When GTA V Was Released - Sports Illustrated
content: José Mourinho’s Manchester United tenure was struggling to get off the ground. The self-proclaimed “special one” had a semblance of juice left in his alluring tank when he arrived at Old Trafford in the summer of 2016, tasked with returning the Red Devils to the promised land. Three successive victories depicted a fast start, but his first roadblock arrived as he encountered old foe Pep Guardiola for the first time in over three years in the Manchester Derby. Guardiola’s City claimed a 2–1 victory, and Watford capitalized on Man Utd’s stumble the following week, beating the Red Devils 3–1. During this early-season blip, Mourinho gunned for his own. The Portuguese backed Gianluca Prestianni to the hilt during the Argentine’s scandal involving Vinícius Júnior earlier this year, when the Brazilian accused Prestianni of racial abuse, but he was out for blood a decade ago. Luke Shaw, Henrikh Mkhitaryan and Jesse Lingard all felt the wrath of their new manager at the start of his reign, so much so that Vice’s Will Magee wrote that Mourinho had gone “full Grand Theft Auto”, comparing him to a “maniacal bus driver with a death wish and a five-star police wanted level.” It’s a hyperbolic description the Real Madrid boss certainly wouldn’t have taken too kindly to, not merely due to its unflattering nature, but because Mourinho is no video game admirer. In 2021, when in charge of Roma, he lamented his players’ habit of staying up all night playing Fortnite, or “that s---”, as he put it. So, the 63-year-old is unlikely to be among those skiving off work after GTA VI’s long-awaited release, and Mourinho would’ve been in a particularly bad mood when the game’s previous iteration dropped a little over 13 years ago. Here’s what Mourinho’s Chelsea team looked like upon GTA V’s release, as the Blues met Basel in their opening Champions League fixture of the 2013–14 season. GK: Petr Čech—Chelsea’s stalwart between the posts was veering toward the end of his tenure with the Blues, and there was nothing he could do to deny Mohamed Salah from drawing the unfancied Basel level in the second half. RB: Branislav Ivanović—Ivanović represented Chelsea almost 400 times, spending nine years in west London. The brutish Serb endured heartbreak and euphoria with the Blues, claiming three Premier League titles and one Champions League. Mourinho would later describe the defender as a “competitive animal” and one of the Blues’ greatest ever signings. CB: Gary Cahill—An unheralded Chelsea figure throughout the 2010s, Cahill played alongside, and would eventually succeed, John Terry at Stamford Bridge. CB: David Luiz—The Brazilian played a surprisingly key role in Chelsea beating Basel in the previous season’s Europa League semifinals. The maverick center back scored in both legs as the Blues secured a 5–2 aggregate victory before going on to defeat Benfica in the final. LB: Ashley Cole—An aging Cole locked horns with Salah, and it’s fair to say the Egyptian got the better of the left back again. Salah had plenty of joy against Cole in their meetings the previous season, and his performances may well have convinced the defender that his time at the highest level was drawing to a close. He left Chelsea at the end of the season. CM: Marco van Ginkel—The young Dutch midfielder joined from Vitesse in the summer, and made his Champions League debut here. Laden with promise, Van Ginkel could’ve been special in west London. However, he’d soon suffer a devastating knee injury that would alter his career trajectory. CM: Frank Lampard—Lampard was one of two Chelsea players who were on the roster for their previous Champions League group stage defeat at Stamford Bridge (2–0 to Beşiktaş in October 2003). The stalwart midfielder captained the Blues against Basel in Terry’s absence, and teed up the opening goal before things went awry in the second half. RW: Willian—He was so close to joining Tottenham Hotspur in the summer until Chelsea swooped in at the last minute. Willian’s Chelsea career would age like a fine wine, with the early stages of his time at Stamford Bridge plagued by inconsistency. This was his debut for the club. AM: Oscar—Oscar was Chelsea’s goalscorer in the 2–1 defeat, having scored five times in the Champions League the previous season. The Brazilian was still in the infancy of his career and seemingly destined for stardom at this point, but his influence waned toward the end of Mourinho’s second tenure, and he agreed to move to China in late 2017. The decision likely cost him a long and successful career at the highest level, but Oscar, who officially retired earlier this year, quickly made peace with the decision he made. LW: Eden Hazard—Hazard built on an impressive debut season in his sophomore year, helping Chelsea escape their early-season rut. The Blues had made the worst start to a Premier League season in a decade, but would recover to finish third, scuppering Liverpool’s title tilt in the process. Hazard finished 2013–14 with 14 league goals, a tally he’d match the following season and improve on in 2016–17 and 2018–19. ST: Samuel Eto’o—Well into the twilight of his career, Eto’o, one of the finest strikers of his generation, was certainly serviceable for the Blues. The Cameroonian great spent just a season at Stamford Bridge, scoring 12 times in 35 appearances, including three in the Champions League as Chelsea reached the semifinals. title: Mac Engel: Debut of TCU’s Robbie Avila v. Texas A&M shows best and worst of college basketball - The Derrick
content: A clear sky. Low near 35F. Winds light and variable.. A clear sky. Low near 35F. Winds light and variable. On Nov. 19, 2026, in Fort Worth, Texas, center Robbie Avila (21) played against Texas A&M in his first game for the school since coming to the team on Nov. 12. (Abigail Dollins/Fort Worth Star-Telegram/TNS) FORT WORTH, Texas — The same fans who booed a Baylor player who walked onto the same floor because both he and the team violated the “spirit” of college basketball had no problem buying tickets and cheering when their school did the same thing. On Thursday night against Texas A&M, fifth-year senior transfer center Robbie Avila made his debut for TCU, an appearance not that much different than what Baylor did with forward James Nnaji. Nnaji was the former 2023 NBA draft pick who came to the Bears at the semester break in January of this year, and made his debut for the team at TCU, which caused the national reaction of, “What are we even doing?” The response to that, as well as everything else in college sports, is not a damn thing. TCU basketball coach Jamie Dixon said then, “Call it what it is; you can be as good as you want to be. We’ve seen that in football. Just put the resources into it.” (When did “resources” become a synonym for “cash?”) Call all of it what it is — a joke, the antithesis of what college sports is supposed to be about. It’s also perfectly “legal” in a world where a rule book only exists to be challenged in court, and any enforced penalty will promptly be overturned by a local judge. As evidenced by the game and the capacity crowd on what was a great night of college basketball in Texas A&M’s 97-92 overtime win over TCU, the sport is not on the precipice of certain death. It remains in desperate need of a few modifications, starting with enforceable rules, because in a remotely logical world of college sports Robbie Avila is not playing for TCU. November and December have never been great draws for college basketball, and now with an influx of neutral-site tournaments all over the country played before eight fans, the visual of the sport can sometimes look awful. TCU hosting Texas A&M showed what the sport can be; 7,000 people packed in a quaint environment watching two good, and well-paid, teams play a tight game. “What about the crowd tonight? It was great. You could feel the energy in the gym. I know we came out on the right side, but everybody should walk away from that game [feeling] there wasn’t a loser in that game,” Texas A&M coach Bucky McMillan said. “It was just a great game. It was great basketball. If you watch these games going on right now in Las Vegas [at the Players Era Festival] with great teams, but there is no one in the crowd. You’ve got to remember this is about these universities. The basketball team is 15 individuals at the university; you can go out to Vegas and be out there with your team and maybe rally around it, but what about it’s here in the state and both universities get to rally around it? With so many good teams we’d like to play more in-state teams, for sure.” Most coaches agree on the concept, but they seldom can agree on the specifics. After TCU played its old Southwest Conference opponent, former Pac-12 rivals Oregon State played Oregon on the West Coast. But the game wasn’t in Eugene or Corvallis, but rather in Portland in an NBA arena before an announced attendance of 5,607. Put the games where they belong, on campus. Give the fans a reason to go to the games with strong, regional matchups and people will show up. The atmosphere inside TCU’s Schollmaier Arena for its game against A&M was undeniably fun. The transfer portal has done permanent damage to roster building and continuity, but college students and fans are still drawn to the game and a decent opponent. “I like it way better than getting on a plane,” McMillan said after the game. “We’ve got so many great schools here in Texas. Just look at the quality of play, and how many [NCAA] tournament teams were from Texas last year.” One day before former University of Michigan coach Dusty May made his regular-season debut with the Dallas Mavericks last month, I asked him what he felt the biggest adjustment between NCAA and NBA basketball will be. His answer was in college he didn’t know who would be on the other team, and preparing was a guessing game. Transfers and player eligibility is damaging, not killing, college basketball. Teams all over the country, including Texas A&M, have a player or two whose presence required a lawyer and a judge. What LSU football coach Lane Kiffin and basketball coach Will Wade are trying to do to get players may make former Louisiana Gov. Huey Long proud, but it’s an embarrassment to the school. “It seems like ‘litigation’ should be a different category (in a box score); rebounding-litigation-points,” Dixon said after the game Between Indiana State and Saint Louis University, Avila played four years of college basketball; he was not selected in the 2026 NBA draft, but he signed a contract with the L.A. Lakers and played for their summer team. Now he’s back in college because he, along with a host of other players who signed pro contracts but didn’t “make it,” was granted a fifth year of eligibility. The Big 12 is loaded with these guys. Because TCU, like so many other schools, offers a variety of degree plans on varying schedules, Avila could easily enroll for classes in the second week of November. He will be here for a little more than five months, and he’s gone. It’s “legal” — whatever that means — but it’s ridiculous. As evidenced by the crowd and atmosphere for Texas A&M at TCU, the sport is hardly dead, but it’s in dire need of modifications, starting with more games like these in November and December on campus. title: Oral arguments held in MCN v. Kunzweiler appeal - MVSKOKE Media
content: DENVER – The United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit heard oral arguments in the appeal of the opinion and order handed down in Muscogee Creek Nation v. Kunzweiler last year. In Nov. 2025, MCN filed a motion for a preliminary injunction against Tulsa County District Attorney Steve Kunzweiler, seeking to prevent him from asserting concurrent criminal jurisdiction over non-Mvskoke Tribal members within the Mvskoke Reservation. As previously reported, the United States District Court for the Northern District of Oklahoma denied this motion. This decision was appealed to the Tenth Circuit, which held oral arguments on the matter on Nov. 17. The appeal was heard by Judges Harris Hartz, David Ebel, and Carolyn McHugh. MCN was represented by Riyaz A. Kanji. Kannon K. Shanmugam represented Kunzweiler. A recording of the oral arguments is available on the Mvskoke Media YouTube channel. Kanji began the arguments by pointing out that three recent cases before the Tenth Circuit have resulted in rulings upholding the longstanding rule that states cannot exercise jurisdiction over Indians in Indian Country. Kanji pointed out that these rulings also matched the statutory enactments that provide that the Indians in question do not have to be members of the Tribe for that Tribe to have jurisdiction over them. Kanji then pointed out that state courts can have jurisdiction over Indians in Indian Country under Public Law 280, but that requires the Tribe in question to consent. Kanji suggested Oklahoma’s attempt to assert unilateral jurisdiction over Indians in Indian Country was not supported by any legal precedent or federal statute. Kanji then addressed the argument that concurrent jurisdiction does not harm Tribal sovereignty. He highlighted that an essential aspect of Tribal decision-making is prosecutorial discretion. Prosecutorial discretion refers to the legal principle that the prosecutor in a case decides whether to charge a person with a crime and what charges to file. Kanji pointed out that when the state claims unilateral jurisdiction over Indians, it renders the Tribal prosecutor’s discretion irrelevant, as the state prosecutor can decide to proceed with prosecution or charge the defendant with different crimes. Kanji referred to a policy instituted by Tulsa Sheriff Vic Regalato that stated that if a Tribal citizen was arrested who as not an MCN citizen, then they would be sent to state court. According to Kanji this was not concurrent jurisdiction, but instead amounted to exclusive jurisdiction. Kanji then noted that a defendant who was sentenced to attend a substance abuse rehab program as a part of Tribal court proceedings could also end up in state jail, which would result in their inability to complete their Tribal court sentence. During Kanji’s arguments, Judge McHugh asked that he address the Castro-Huerta decision. Judge Hugh pointed out that the decision seemed to indicate a presumption of concurrent jurisdiction. Kanji answered that the decision stated that states exercise jurisdiction except where preempted by federal law or the principles of Tribal self-government. Kanji reiterated that in the Castro-Huerta case, the state was not prosecuting Indians, so there was no conflict of concurrent jurisdiction. Shanmugam represented Kunzweiler and began his arguments by asserting that the Castro-Huerta decision gave the state jurisdiction over non-Indian defendants on the Mvskoke Reservation. Shanmugam asserted that there is no legal difference between a non-Indian defendant and a non-Mvskoke Indian defendant on the Mvskoke Reservation. Judge McHugh pointed out that Congress uses the language “Indians” to refer to all Indians, not members of a particular Tribe. Shanmugam stated that when Congress amended the Indian Civil Rights Act in 1991 to explicitly confer jurisdiction on Tribal governments over non-member Indians, it did not intend to strip the state of jurisdiction over the same defendants. This amendment is referred to as the “Duro-Fix” after the Supreme Court decision in Duro v. Reina. Judge Hartz pointed out that, since Congress was conferring jurisdiction on Tribes in these instances, it can be inferred that Congress did not intend for the states to have jurisdiction. Judge McHugh stated that courts have ruled that states lack jurisdiction over Indians. McHugh said, “You don’t have to strip it, if it never existed.” Shanmugam argued that it is not a settled proposition and that the assumption that states do not have jurisdiction was not codified in law. Judge Hartz asked if historical Supreme Court decisions reflected a hostility toward states exercising jurisdiction over Indians in Indian Territory regardless of Tribal membership. Shanmugam conceded that was correct, but asserted that the Court has moved away from that position in the modern era. Shanmugam stated that there are not many cases concerning the prosecution of non-member Indians. In his view, the prosecution of non-member Indians was an edge case until the McGirt decision. Shanmugam suggested that the Supreme Court wants lower courts to address the question of jurisdiction on the Mvskoke Reservation using the Castro-Huerta framework. Judge McHugh asked why Shanmugam would cite the Bracker balancing test referenced in Castro-Huerta, when Bracker explicitly states that it is to be applied when the defendant is a non-Indian. Shanmugam argued that Bracker is about balancing the sovereign interests of the federal government, the state, and the Tribe. The state has a sovereign interest to ensure public safety within its territory. According to Shanmugam, the Tribe has less interest in the matter, because non-member Indians are not the Tribe’s constituents. Shanmugam denied that concurrent jurisdiction usurped Tribal prosecutorial discretion. Judge Hartz then pointed out that concurrent jurisdiction would have significant legal implications when prosecutors have differing opinions on how a case should be charged or prosecuted. Shanmugam agreed with this assertion and replied that concurrent jurisdiction exists practically in various forms and there are instances where all three sovereigns have jurisdiction. As an example, he used cases under the Violence Against Women Act, where in certain instances Congress conferred jurisdiction over non-Indians to Tribal governments. According to Shanmugam, these are examples of competing sovereign interests, and the state’s interests would be eliminated if it had no authority to prosecute. Judge Hartz observed that Shanmugam seemed to be discounting the Tribal interests. Shanmugam denied this and stated that if the state retained jurisdiction over non-member Indians, both the Tribe and state would be able to address their sovereign interests. Shanmugam asserted that if the Northern District ruling was overturned, the state would lose its ability to address its sovereign interests. Judge Hartz asked whether Shanmugam believed there was relevant dicta from the Supreme Court in McGirt. Dicta, in a legal sense, refers to comments, observations, or suggestions made by a judge in an opinion that are not necessary to resolve the case and do not establish legal precedent. Shanmugam stated that if there is dicta in the McGirt decision, it is weak. Judge Hartz pushed back on this assertion, pointing out that McGirt was a Seminole Nation citizen. Shanmugam pointed out that the McGirt case dealt with the Major Crimes Act, so it was not applicable. Judge McHugh asked whether, if the court upheld the Northern District Court’s ruling, states where Public Law 280 applied would have jurisdiction over non-member Indians. Shanmugam stated they would. He then reiterated that MCN did not have Tribal self-governing interests in the case because the Indians in question were not Mvskoke citizens. Judge Ebel asked if there was an agreed-upon definition of who is or is not an Indian and, if so, what case it is in. Shanmugam did not know of a case and pointed out that Tribes determine their own membership with consultation with the BIA. Judge Ebel pointed out that Tribal membership could be a very different issue from whether you are considered an Indian or not. Judge Ebel asked whether Shanmugam had any guidance on the issue, and Shanmugam deferred to Kanji. Judge Ebel asked whether there was an accepted definition, and Shanmugam stated that he did not think there was Judge Ebel pointed out that if the court ruled that MCN had jurisdiction over Indians on the Mvskoke Reservation, state officials would have no way of determining who was an Indian for jurisdictional purposes. Judge McHugh then asked Kanji, at the beginning of his rebuttal, whether there was a definition of “Indian” that is routinely applied under the law. Kanji stated that the court has addressed the question many times; it is a two-pronged definition that requires some degree of Indian blood and some recognition by the Tribe. Judge Ebel asked if the degree of Indian blood had been defined. Kanji stated no. Judge Ebel asked who gets to define it, and Kanji stated that it was a combination of the Tribes and the BIA. In closing, Kanji focused on four main points. The first was that the Duro-Fix was enacted because states lack presumed jurisdiction over Indians regardless of Tribal membership. His second point was that Castro-Huerta delineates two ways for pre-emptive jurisdiction: ordinary federal pre-emption and pre-emption under Tribal self-government. His third point was that Oklahoma was not different from other states that had Tribal populations or reservations, and there was a long legal history of states trying to illegally assert jurisdiction over Indians. His final point was that the MCN has a robust legal system funded at a higher per-capita level than Tulsa County’s, and it is working well, according to testimony in the case from local police chiefs. Kanji argued that this was evidence that concurrent jurisdiction is not necessary to maintain public safety because the MCN is addressing that state sovereign interest in regard to non-member Indians. Finally, Kanji pointed out the fact that this case deals only with one sheriff and one district attorney in one county. According to Kanji, the vast majority of other counties and cities in the Mvskoke Reservation are respecting MCN rights and are cooperating. title: Coco Gauff, Ann Li to Launch USA v. Hungary BJK Cup Playoff - Tennis Now
content: Coco Gauff and Ann Li launch Team USA's Billie Jean King Cup Playoff tie on Saturday. By Richard Pagliaro | Friday, November 20, 2026Photo credit: Manuela Davies/USTA Delray Beach native Coco Gauff will hit the homecoming court tomorrow. Two-time Grand Slam champion Gauff will face Hungarian Dalma Galfi in the opener of the best-of-five match United States vs. Hungary Billie Jean King Cup Playoff at the Delray Beach Tennis Center tomorrow. “I haven’t played Dalma in like a tournament or anything. I’ve watched her play a few times,” Gauff said. “I think when you’re playing on tour, we kind of all know each other’s games and stuff. Obviously we’ll do more scouting tonight with my team and stuff to prepare for tomorrow. “As far as being like a player ranked higher, the favorite, I don’t believe in favorites in sports. I think we all have an equal opportunity to win that day. It’s just all about who can perform better that day. Obviously I guess the numbers are on my side. I hope real life reality is on my side, too.” Billie Jean King Cup debutant Ann Li will follow against Hungarian No. 1 Anna Bondar in Saturday’s second singles match. “I think my season was great. I started off a little slow, but ended really well,” Li told the media in Delray Beach. “Yeah, I learned a lot about myself, grew a lot as a player and as a person. “This is my first time here representing USA. I’m so excited to play for Lindsay [Davenport], so excited to play alongside these girls. Hopefully bring my best tennis to finish this year off.” Desirae Krawczyk and US Open doubles champion Taylor Townsend are the nominated U.S. doubles team and will lead off on Sunday vs. Bondar and Fanny Stollar. Gauff will then take the court against the 76th-ranked Bondar with Li scheduled to play world No. 155 Galfi in the last match of the tie. The first nation to win three matches over the weekend clinches victory and will be one of seven nations advancing out of the Playoffs to the 2027 Qualifiers. title: Xavier v. Iowa: Preview, matchups, keys to the game - Banners On The Parkway
content: Xavier hosts one of the darlings of the 2026 NCAA Tournament to kick off a key stretch, Xavier won on Tuesday. They did it in such a fashion that their KenPom ranking dropped 13 positions post game. The Musketeers shot poorly, defended in lackluster fashion, and generally gave off full trap game vibes. The reason for that is this game. Xavier played Mississippi State in what appeared to be a repurposed conference hall, then had CSU, and now has Iowa. This is a Sweet Sixteen type of game. Xavier is coming off an NIT performance. But you’ll have that and X did win. Iowa took a slightly different tack on Sunday in that they played poorly and then lost. Creighton forced the Hawkeyes into a 23.4% turnover rate that complimented Iowa’s very poor shooting night quite nicely. Both teams come into this game, then, having played the one prior poorly. Xavier stumbled into a trap, Iowa ran into a decent team. The metrics weren’t impressed with either. Add Banners On The Parkway as a preferred source to see more of our reporting on Google. For Xavier this is a chance to build a resume. The Musketeers can’t rely on the Big East to bail them out like they could in the past. Every team is in the KenPom top 100 now, but Seton Hall looks an awful lot like Xavier last year thus far, and Butler is still Butler. X has four games against top 50 opponents in the next two weeks. Three of those are against top 25 teams, even. Now is the time to stack something that will matter come March. Iowa plays slow. Like, two from lowest adjusted tempo in the nation slow. On offense they are incredibly efficient inside, grab an unholy 42% of their own misses, and get to the line a ton. They take, but don’t make, a lot of threes. It’s going to be a long defensive grind to get the ball back once the Hawkeyes have it. Unless, of course, they turn it over. They do that a lot for a team that plays so slowly. Defensively they also want to slow the game down. They neither surrender a lot of three point attempts nor three point makes. They can be had inside, but they’ll make it take awhile to get there. The Hawkeyes don’t block shots, but they are also elite at preventing second chances. Their defensive profile is somewhat unusual to say the least. Iowa gets a lot of minutes from their bench, although some of that has been enforced by injury and ineffectiveness in the starting lineup. Backup point Ty’Reek Coleman has a case for being the most effective guard on the roster. He is lightning quick and gets to the rim extremely well, where he has shot 13-16 on the season. He is 2-9 in other field goal attempts so staying in front of this guy is pretty vital. Second on the team in minutes off the bench is freshman Peyton McCollum, who is the son of Iowa head coach Ben McCollum. He did well in the buy games, but in 41 minutes in the past two games he has 8 points on 3-8 from the floor. 6’11” big man Trevin Jirak had been pretty absent, but broke out against Creighton with 22/6/4 in just 21 minutes to stake his claim to some of the minutes down low, especially if McKeever still isn’t 100%. Freshman guard Jaidyn Coon is still finding his feet at this level, but he was very effective against Creighton with 7 points on 2-3 from the floor in 11 minutes. Big man Cam Manyawu is in his third year playing under McCollum and had started all 75 games in that span until Sunday against Creighton, when he managed just 3 minutes off the bench. He is not listed on any injury reports, but it seems his poor start to the season had placed him outside the circle of trust for the time being at least. - Trap game or harbinger? Coach Pitino was quick to call the Cleveland State no-show a trap game. That’s a lot easier for a coach to say than “yeah, they figured out we can’t shoot and came up with a really good strategy based on that.” Iowa usually stretches out to prevent three point shooting. If they come out and sit back a bit, you’ll know they watched a lot of film. - Who can step up this time? It was Rolyns Aligbe last time. Hopefully Xavier’s stars play better, but the bench depth has been key thus far. There is no word on Nikos Chitikoudis yet and X will need someone to fill in that role down low. - Can Xavier shoot at all? It has been bad so far. If this is what X is, they aren’t going to go far. Teams that shoot 29% behind the arc generally aren’t a threat to advance all that far in the tournament or win big non-conference games. Xavier needs to find someone, anyone, that can consistently make an outside shot. If they don’t this, and other big games to come, will not go well. title: This New 3-Row Honda SUV Hints at the Next-Gen CR-V with Modern Styling and New Hybrid Powertrain - Car and Driver
content: The Avancier is a three-row SUV that won’t be sold in the U.S. market, but it gives us an idea of what to expect with Honda’s upcoming hybrid product blitz. Honda has revealed the second-generation Avancier today, and while it won’t be offered in the United States, the new SUV gives us a preview of the upcoming next-generation CR-V and other hybrid models due out over the next few years. Designed for Asian markets such as Thailand, Japan, and China, the three-row Avancier sits above the CR-V and pairs clean, modern styling with a new hybrid powertrain. The Avancier debuts Honda’s new two-motor hybrid powertrain, called Honda Hybrid. For now, Honda is remaining tight-lipped about many of the details. The automaker promises “excellent fuel economy,” and the Avancier also launches Honda’s new DualPower eAWD system, controlling the front and rear wheels independently via separate electric motors. The S+ Shift function, which simulates gearshifts for the hybrid powertrain and has been seen on the Civic Hybrid and Prelude, is also present. The Avancier is also the first Honda that is not an EV to feature the brand’s latest “H” logo, which was introduced in 2024 and was originally set to be used exclusively for electric models. With Honda cancelling its trio of EVs that were meant to be built in Ohio—the Acura RSX and Honda 0-Series Saloon and 0-Series SUV—the company has decided to roll out the simplified “H” logo across its entire lineup starting in 2027. The new badge sits proudly on the nose of the Avancier, just below a thin opening that connects the squinting LED daytime running lights. The main headlights sit below, linked by a series of geometric trim pieces that, along with a vent in the lower bumper, help channel air to the engine. The side profile of the Avancier is clean, with flush door handles and gloss black trim that frames the wheel arches and the bottom of the SUV. Around back, the taillights consist of blocky, vertical elements connected by a light bar. While we don’t think the next CR-V will look exactly like the Avancier, we expect to see elements such as the thin DRLs to migrate across the Honda lineup in the coming years. The cabin will also likely inform future U.S.-bound Hondas, and it gives off an airy, tranquil vibe. Unfortunately, the Avancier appears to have skipped out on most physical controls, putting nearly every function into the sizable screen that sits above the air vents in the center of the dashboard. We hope Honda reconsiders this approach in the U.S., given how much we appreciate the intuitive, straightforward physical buttons and knobs found in current Hondas. The Avancier also introduces a column-mounted shifter, a feature we also tested on a next-generation Civic prototype we drove last year. It frees up space on the center console. The steering wheel has an unusual squared-off shape with a flat bottom, and behind it there is a digital gauge cluster. Glowing ambient lighting and white upholstery create a futuristic, sterile appearance, and a panoramic glass roof extends all the way to the third row. Honda loaded the SUV with premium features, such as heated and ventilated seats in the second row and a 12-speaker Bose stereo with Dolby Atmos. There’s also a system that uses cameras on the inside and outside of the Avancier to let owners check on the cabin and car’s surroundings remotely via a smartphone app. While the Avancier won’t be sold on our shores, we expect to see elements of its styling on upcoming Hondas, as well as its new hybrid powertrain. Honda plans to launch 15 new hybrid models globally by 2030, which includes a new CR-V next year, as well as a new Civic and a heavily updated Accord in the near future. Caleb Miller began blogging about cars at 13 years old, and he realized his dream of writing for a car magazine after graduating from Carnegie Mellon University and joining the Car and Driver team. He loves quirky and obscure autos, aiming to one day own something bizarre like a Nissan S-Cargo, and is an avid motorsports fan. title: Émile V. Schlesser on Backstage: Making Power Visible Through Performance and Colour - Indie Shorts Mag
content: Follow Indie Shorts Mag on WhatsApp for the latest news and updates on short  film festivals and short films. ReadFilm News In Backstage, a young actor’s opportunity to work with an influential theatre director becomes a study of ambition, manipulation and the difficulty of saying no. Drawing on a personal experience from his early years as an actor, Luxembourg filmmaker Émile V. Schlesser worked with co-writer Jonas Brand to explore how an abusive relationship can develop through gestures that initially seem harmless. In this conversation with Indie Shorts Mag, Schlesser discusses the trust behind the performances, the film’s carefully defined colour palette and the resourcefulness required to bring it to the screen. From selling paintings to help finance the production to recording improvised jazz against the projected film, he offers a detailed look at the choices that shaped Backstage. Indie Shorts Mag: It took you almost a decade to understand the experience that inspired Backstage and recognise that you did not need to keep blaming yourself. How did that distance shape the perspective from which you wanted to tell the young actor’s story? ReadFilm News Émile V. Schlesser: I hope it helped me craft a believable and relatable story about how an abusive relationship unfolds. In hindsight, having experienced something similar, I can recognise the tactics a person would use to manipulate. When you’re going through it, you’re often unaware of these almost invisible mechanisms. What makes it so difficult to realise is that it usually begins with the smallest gestures. First, a compliment here and there. Then, gradually more transgressive actions. Yet always subtle enough to keep you wondering how that person actually meant it. Because there’s no clear threat in the beginning, it’s difficult to resist or fight back. You don’t want to cause trouble, so you pretend everything’s fine. But once you’ve missed the opportunity to say “no”, the abuser may interpret your silence as consent and continue crossing one boundary after another. Eventually, when you do start pushing back, the abuser may gaslight you into believing that you’re the one to blame since you started it by having played along. Indie Shorts Mag: How did you and co-writer Jonas Brand approach making the gradual development of an abusive relationship believable within the compressed form of a short film? Émile V. Schlesser: Jonas and I really wanted to avoid an oversimplified portrayal of victimhood and culpability. We didn’t want anything black and white. Instead, we wanted to explore the ambiguous grey areas, contradictions and subtle shifts in power that make abusive relationships so impenetrable and disorienting. This felt much closer to how these things actually unfold in real life. Choosing to show a female abuser allowed us to explore forms of manipulation that are completely different to the methods usually used by men. Much more complex and less straightforward. Cosima can be gentle, warm and sweet, seductive and motherly. She knows when to appear small and vulnerable, seemingly offering Lukas the position of power while giving him a false sense of security. This completely messes with his mind, making it so much more devious and perfidious. But also so much more interesting to watch. Indie Shorts Mag: What made the dynamic between a young man and an older female authority figure important to the way you wanted Backstage to explore power and vulnerability? Émile V. Schlesser: One of the reasons we chose to make the protagonist a young man being abused by an older woman (apart from the fact that it’s based on a real-life event) was to further encourage men in the audience to connect and sympathise with the victim. Undoubtedly, most women in the audience know what it feels like to be caught in such a situation. But men? Maybe not so much. By telling the story this way, I think a wider audience might be able to recognise how these situations develop and how easily they can happen. Another important reason was that my co-writer Jonas Brand and I were keen on exploring the ambiguity and sneaky moral grey areas. We wanted to create relatable characters caught in a complex situation that would leave audiences with enough uncertainty to keep questioning and discussing long after the screening. Whose fault is it, really? It’s not that clear-cut. Lukas isn’t simply a victim, while Cosima, although deeply flawed, possesses many relatable traits that make it possible for an audience to empathise with her. We felt that portraying a predator as an almost sympathetic character, while never losing sight of the harm they cause or excusing their actions, was only possible if that character was a woman. No one wants to watch a film that asks them to see poor old Harvey as a complex, ambiguous figure they might actually feel sorry for. Indie Shorts Mag: Philippe Delacroix’s success follows his appearance in Cosima’s previous play. How did you approach his character’s role in establishing what a young actor like Lukas might feel is at stake when working with her? Émile V. Schlesser: For Lukas, Philippe’s fate serves as both a warning and a promise. On one hand, the realisation that Philippe owes his highly successful career to Cosima’s power and goodwill could be very alluring to a young, ambitious actor like Lukas, who is hungry enough and willing to consider making that same bargain. Cosima understands the power of this temptation and actively exploits it for her own personal benefit. On the other hand, we get a sense that Philippe is still traumatised by the deal he made with Cosima and the emotional harm it caused. He has in effect sold his integrity, his body, his soul. Even after all these years, he still feels controlled by and indebted to his abuser. In that sense, Philippe embodies both the seductive promise of what Cosima can offer and the devastating price that comes with accepting it. Indie Shorts Mag: Jonathan Joèl Albrecht plays a young actor who is himself performing onstage. How did you work with him to distinguish those layers of performance while keeping the character’s emotional experience clear? Émile V. Schlesser: Jonathan – as well as Jil Devresse, who plays his acting partner – has experience on the theater stage, so he was already well equipped to navigate these different acting styles. The challenge was switching between the colourful, artificial, theatrical style of the play and the much subtler, intimate naturalism of film acting. Both had to work simultaneously on an actual stage and in front of the camera, often with the camera right up in their faces. “Python”, the play they are performing in the film, already portrays an abusive relationship between a man and a woman. So, things quickly become quite “meta”, as it gets harder to differentiate between play and real life. Over the course of the film, it becomes increasingly difficult to tell Cosima’s unorthodox directing methods apart from actual abuse. We used this confusion to further blur Lukas’ assessment of the situation, making it increasingly difficult for him to see clearly what’s happening to him. Indie Shorts Mag: How did you work with Sascha Ley on Cosima’s glances, smiles and small gestures to convey the control she exerts over Lukas? Émile V. Schlesser: In preparation, as Sascha and I were developing Cosima’s personality, we made sure never to judge her character, even if, objectively speaking, her actions are inexcusable. The truth is, no one sees themselves as a villain. We all have our reasons, motivations and justifications for the way we behave. What really made it interesting was considering the possibility of what would happen if Cosima were actually in love with Lukas. This would make her susceptible to misinterpreting his reactions and mixed signals as signs that he feels the same way. In the beginning, he may indeed genuinely enjoy her attention and feel flattered that someone of her standing takes such an interest in him. She, on the other hand, is completely oblivious to the fact that, given the power imbalance, it would be very hard for him to communicate his discomfort in any way. When things finally escalate, Cosima is genuinely stunned when Lukas pushes her away. From her one-sided perspective, it seemed as though there had been consent. She does have a point when she spits out, “You should have said no earlier.” But that’s exactly the dilemma. It’s not that simple. Indie Shorts Mag: What did creating a safe working environment mean in practice when directing Jonathan Joèl Albrecht and Sascha Ley through a story about manipulation and control? Émile V. Schlesser: The single most important thing on this production was trust. We did not have an intimacy coordinator on set – which, I know, might seem strange on a project with a topic like this. I talked a lot with my cast members, and together we realised that we had built so much trust between us that the actors didn’t feel the need for an intimacy coordinator. They actually felt more comfortable without an outside third party intervening. For me, it’s all about what my actors want and need to feel safe, so I respected their wishes. In any case, as a director, I believe it is vital to create a positive and creative working environment in which everyone feels safe, respected, and supported. Indie Shorts Mag: Jil Devresse plays the acting partner who witnesses what unfolds. How did you approach that character’s perspective as a way for the audience to understand the central relationship? Émile V. Schlesser: Jil’s character, Vero, is the silent observer. She might seem passive, yes, but I believe this character is arguably the one most of us can identify with. We’ve all heard or even witnessed stories about people in positions of authority misusing their power to manipulate and abuse – and have chosen not to act, staying silent instead. I believe most people either turn a blind eye or are reluctant to step in to help for various reasons. It can also be insensitive to pressure a victim into speaking up when they themselves might not even know fully grasp what’s happening to them. In Vero’s case, we can tell she clearly has a hunch. She knows about Cosima’s past as an abuser and accepts it as part of the industry’s game. There is one scene, though, where she subtly gives Lukas the opportunity to open up and tell her the truth – but he chooses not to. Indie Shorts Mag: How did your background in visual art inform your collaboration with cinematographer Thorsten on developing the visual language of Backstage within a working theatre? Émile V. Schlesser: Working with Thorsten Harms, my DP, was so easy, as we speak the same language in terms of visual grammar. We were on the same page from the get-go and had a lot of fun working out ways to convey power balance within the frame through blocking and staging. For instance, we enjoyed playing with lines in the composition and how actors would cross them within the frame as they moved around in a scene. The moment of their first kiss is a good example for this. Indie Shorts Mag: What guided your use of the colour palette to communicate the balance of power between Lukas and Cosima in Backstage? Émile V. Schlesser: Thorsten and I carefully worked out a colour code that would help tell the story on a purely visual, visceral level. We narrowed it down to red, blue, and gold, giving each a specific meaning and using them very consciously throughout the film. Red symbolises abuse and gradually appears more and more as the story unfolds. Blue, by contrast, represents liberation. The two colours are in constant dialogue with one another throughout the film. Lighting was another important part of our visual grammar. Whenever Lukas is being seduced, for example, we use a cosy, golden light to make the atmosphere feel warm and inviting. This creates a false sense of security, and an emotional dissonance with the tension, disgust and anxiety that Lukas (and the audience) are actually feeling in these moments. Indie Shorts Mag: You sold paintings to help finance Backstage and had only one week of access to the theatre. How did you decide which creative elements needed protecting as you allocated the production’s limited resources? Émile V. Schlesser: I knew this story needed real production value for it to work. The audience has to feel that there’s a lot at stake for Lukas. You have to believe that Cosima is indeed a highly successful director of international renown, someone who has the power to make or break his career. If you don’t get a real sense that this is Lukas’ big breakout opportunity, it becomes much harder to relate to his reluctance to push back against Cosima’s advances. So, elements like shooting in a lavish location and having enough extras to sell the illusion of a sold-out theatre were a must. Since we couldn’t secure any funding from official institutions, I tried to maximise production value in every detail without spending money we didn’t have. This included costumes, props, production design, but also extras. In the end, we had to cheat a little using optical tricks. For example, the crowd shot during the theatre premiere was a composite shot. We only had around 30 extras sitting there, but we made it look like 300. Indie Shorts Mag: Having taken on the editing yourself, what did working with the footage reveal about the performances that was harder to recognise while directing on set? Émile V. Schlesser: When you sit down in a relaxed environment to edit the material you’ve shot, you inevitably notice details and nuances in the performances that you simply couldn’t catch when you’re immersed in the chaotic frenzy of production. Oftentimes, an actor’s instinct on their first take is what turns out to have the most resonance – before the director steps in and crams their heads with too much information. In that sense, I have to say that both Jonathan and Sascha made my life as an editor really hard. They gave such strong performances. There were so many great takes to choose from, all different in colour, but each filled to the brim with raw, truthful emotion. Making the right choices wasn’t easy, but that’s a luxury problem I love to have. Indie Shorts Mag: How did you and composer Rickie Lee Kroell develop the relationship between the score and the edit to create Backstage’s sense of isolation? Émile V. Schlesser: Creating the music with Rickie was a truly unique experience. First, we didn’t feel the film needed a traditional score, as the tension really lies in the quiet moments and awkward silences. But the diegetic music played on stage eventually turns into a sort of score as soon as we cut to the action behind the curtain. The way Rickie recorded it was especially exciting. She invited two jazz musicians, a bassist and a drummer (the latter being her father), to improvise freely in response to the film’s dynamics as it was being projected on a screen. Their improvisation was recorded live on the spot, already synced to the image. Nothing had been written beforehand, and the musicians hadn’t seen the film before the recording. We did it the way Miles Davis and Louis Malle did in 1958 for “Elevator to the Gallows”, and we all thought it was the coolest thing ever. Indie Shorts Mag: What do you hope Backstage encourages audiences to reconsider about why someone may struggle to say no to a person in authority? Émile V. Schlesser: Anyone can be abused – and anyone can be an abuser. Men and women alike. If you haven’t lived through a similar situation, it’s easy to look at it from the outside and judge the victims, thinking, “That would never happen to me.” But it really isn’t that simple. So many factors can make it difficult to even recognise that you’re being manipulated or taken advantage of. And once you do realise what’s going on, it can feel like it’s already too late to speak up. On one hand, what’s paralyzing you is fear – the fear of losing career opportunities, being punished, or provoking the abuser’s temper. On the other hand, it can also be love, admiration, or friendship. You may feel close to the person, or believe you’ve had a good collaboration, and simply don’t want to hurt their feelings. And the longer you avoid taking action, seeking help, or clearly communicating how you feel, the messier it gets. Schlesser’s reflections on Backstage connect its examination of power with the practical work of filmmaking: directing layered performances, composing images, shaping an edit and finding ways to give limited resources a convincing scale. His account also places trust at the centre of collaboration, describing the conversations that helped the cast feel supported while exploring difficult material. For filmmakers, the interview offers a close look at how artistic choices can carry a story’s meaning. For audiences, it returns to the question running through the film: what makes it so difficult to recognise an abuse of power, and to speak when a boundary has been crossed? title: Newcastle v Arsenal: Key stats and talking points - Yahoo Sports
content: BBC Sport examines some of the key themes before Saturday's match, with Arsenal targeting a sixth consecutive league win. Newcastle scored six goals in their first three Premier League home games under Matthias Jaissle but have drawn a blank in their two subsequent matches at St James' Park, losing 1-0 to Aston Villa and Everton. In fact, the Magpies have gone 263 minutes since their last goal on Tyneside, netted by Lewis Hall to put them 2-0 ahead after seven minutes against Hull City on 19 September. Jaissle was left with mixed emotions after the draw at Fulham a fortnight ago, calling the performance "a step in the right direction" but bemoaning the "slapstick" nature of the Cottagers' equaliser, which came just three minutes after Jacob Murphy's spectacular 80th-minute opener. Newcastle have already lost a joint-high seven top-flight home games this calendar year and the omens suggest they may struggle against Arsenal. The Magpies have failed to score in 32 Premier League games against the Gunners - the most by a side against one opponent in the competition's history. Their record against elite teams also offers little encouragement. Newcastle have not beaten the reigning champions since a 2-1 win over Manchester City in 2019 and have just one victory from their past 29 Premier League games against sides starting the day top. Arsenal's tally of five goals conceded is not only the lowest in the Premier League but also the lowest across Europe's top five leagues, a record achieved without key centre-back William Saliba playing at all. The Frenchman, who has been sidelined with a back injury since the World Cup, returned to the matchday squad against Slavia Prague on 4 November but was not involved against Hull City three days later. With summer signing Ezri Konsa deputising admirably, there is no need to rush Saliba back into the starting line-up. The reigning champions have won five consecutive league games, keeping clean sheets in the past four - they have not won five top-flight matches in a row without conceding since 1987. Their supporters love to chant "one-nil to the Arsenal", and that has regularly been the case under Mikel Arteta, with the Gunners winning 34 Premier League games by that scoreline since his appointment in December 2019 - more than any other side. Gunners fans making the long journey to Tyneside are unlikely to return home much before midnight, but after that the team won't venture beyond the capital again for almost two months. The 11 league and cup games that follow will be played either at Emirates Stadium or away to a local rival, with their next scheduled fixture outside of London at Hull City on 16 January.

title: Man City v Fulham: Key stats and talking points - Yahoo Sports
content: After losing three league games on the spin, Manchester City will look to get back to winning ways against improving Fulham. BBC Sport takes a look at some of the key themes going into Saturday's meeting at Etihad Stadium. After suffering three straight league defeats, the arrival at the Etihad Stadium of Fulham will be most welcome by Manchester City. Their run of 20 consecutive wins over the Cottagers is the longest winning streak a team has had against another in English football history. Seventeen of those have been in league fixtures, with City scoring at least twice in all of them. Enzo Maresca's side desperately need to steady the ship after a galling three weeks in which they have gone from being three points clear of Arsenal at the top of the table to six points behind in the space of just 270 minutes of football. After defeats by Brighton, Aston Villa and their 3-1 humbling at Nottingham Forest, City have become only the second team in English top-flight history – after Sheffield Wednesday in 1904-05 – to win their first seven games of a season and then lose the next three. Those losses are as many as they had suffered in their previous 36 top-flight matches, while since the start of the 2007-08 season they have only lost four league games in a row on two occasions - in August 2008 and December 2024. Their defence has really wobbled in recent weeks. After losing to Arsenal in the Community Shield they kept four clean sheets in six matches, but have since shipped 20 goals in their past 10 games. Individual errors have become a problem, while Maresca will have been working hard on stopping his side being so open to counter-attacks - an issue that started under Pep Guardiola last season. They gave up the most shots after fast breaks in the top flight in 2025-26 (39) and so far in this campaign have conceded 19 shots and four goals via fast breaks. Resurgent Fulham arrive in Manchester on the back of a four-match unbeaten run in the league. Firmly finding their feet under Arvelo Arbeloa, the Cottagers are now looking up rather than down after shaking off such a rocky start. Having opened their campaign with three straight defeats they have been beaten in just one of their subsequent seven, and that only came after dramatically throwing away a lead to lose late on against Ipswich Town. While Josh King has garnered most of the attention this season, Alex Iwobi is enjoying a fine campaign of his own. Only Brighton's Pascal Gross has created more chances than the Nigerian's 24 in the top flight and he is also second for defensive line-breaking passes with 39. However, frustratingly for Fulham fans, his creativity is yet to result in an assist which is hardly surprising given only Sunderland and Nottingham Forest have scored fewer goals so far. Given Manchester City come into this game in such poor form, this match surely presents Fulham with their best chance of ending their extraordinary run of defeats against them. The Cottagers have failed to keep a clean sheet in their past 32 Premier League matches against City and have conceded a total of 80 goals in those fixtures. You have to go all the way back to their first visit to the Etihad in 2004, when Edwin van der Sar, was in goal for the last time they kept City out.

title: Aston Villa v Sunderland: Key stats and talking points - Yahoo Sports
content: Unai Emery will take charge of his 150th Premier League game for Aston Villa on Saturday, just two shy of Martin O'Neill's club record. Opponents Sunderland moved off the foot of the table by beating Chelsea last time out but are winless in seven visits to Villa Park, since a 1-0 victory in January 2011. In twice surrendering a two-goal lead during the frenetic 4-4 draw at Old Trafford, Aston Villa again demonstrated they currently lack the trait their manager craves above all: control. The player churn over the summer has given Emery's remodelled side a different feel - more dynamic in attack but less compact defensively, and lacking the nous to dictate play and protect a lead. Despite Emery preaching a patient approach, Villa have too often been drawn into chaotic, end-to-end combat. That jarring with Emery's methodology has caused inconsistency, reflected by the team's mid-table position. Villa have dropped six points in the past five league games and conceded 11 goals during a four-match winless run. They have faced the second most shots in the Premier League this season, made a division-high 18 errors leading to shots and have lost possession within 40 metres of their own goal more often than any side bar Brentford. They are also passive out of possession, with only three teams allowing their opponents to make more passes before attempting to win the ball. Villa have regressed since last season in all of these defensive metrics, and more. They can ill afford for that to continue if they are to challenge for European qualification. Second-bottom Sunderland are vying to win successive league games for the first time since May, with head coach Regis le Bris believing the home victory over Chelsea "embodied the identity, the intensity, the togetherness" which brought a seventh-place finish last season. Enzo le Fee's winning penalty means five of Sunderland's eight top-flight goals in 2026-27 have come from set-pieces; a league-high proportion of 63%. Wasteful finishing from open play has plagued them all season, an issue accentuated by pivotal target man Brian Brobbey missing out this weekend because of a thigh injury. Sunderland's poor away form is another ongoing problem. The Black Cats have only earned one point on their travels this season, at Brentford in September. It's no blip – their Premier League away record over the past 12 months is the worst among the division's 17 ever-present sides across this campaign and last. They have conceded an unrivalled 36 away goals during that period too, with their only clean sheet coming in a 1-0 win at Leeds United in March.

title: Coventry v Crystal Palace: Key stats and talking points - Yahoo Sports
content: It's Frank versus Frank this weekend, as Thomas Frank takes charge of Crystal Palace for the first time against Frank Lampard's Coventry City. Coventry have largely struggled on their return to the Premier League and seven defeats from their opening 10 matches represents their worst start to a league campaign for 106 years. But, despite that statistic, there remains a few reasons for optimism. The Sky Blues have recovered from four straight losses to notch three wins from their past six games – that's more victories than six top-flight teams have mustered this season, including Manchester United and Saturday's visitors. Some of Lampard's players are also starting to look like they belong at this level. Teenage defender Stephen Mfuni, winger Tatsuhiro Sakamoto and star midfielder Jack Rudoni have all impressed in recent weeks, and the latter leads his team-mates in a host of important metrics, such as goals scored and chances created. Attack-minded midfielder Rudoni, who is known to his team-mates as Rudi, has enjoyed learning from his former idol turned head coach Lampard, stating last year that "there's no-one better for me to learn from". Lampard knows exactly what it takes to score goals from midfield and he predicted Rudoni's rise to the top last season. "He's a special player and I really believe he can go as far as he wants," said the Coventry boss in April. Coventry's number five will also have an extra point to prove on Saturday. The 25-year-old hails from Carshalton in south London – a 20-minute drive from Selhurst Park – and he was released by Palace at the age of 11. Bottom-of-the-table Crystal Palace have turned to former Brentford and Tottenham boss Frank to replace Pierre Sage, whose tenure lasted just 16 games. Palace chairman Steve Parish said Frank has a "proven track record of both creating winning teams and improving players, making him the perfect fit for our club". He also fits the club in terms of the 3-5-2 formation preferred by the previous two managers and Frank has deployed wing-backs in almost 40% of his top-flight matches. Whatever formation Frank chooses, he will know the defence requires immediate attention as no side has conceded more than Palace's 24 goals this season. Ten of the past 15 teams to ship 24 goals or more in their opening 10 Premier League games have been relegated, However, the most recent side to let in 24 or more at this stage of the campaign was Wolves – with 27 in 2024-25 – and they finished 16th. The 53-year-old Dane may also want to note that the famed 'new manager bounce' doesn't usually apply to those working at Crystal Palace. Seven of the Eagles' 13 previous permanent managers have lost their first Premier League game in charge and only two have won - Alan Pardew against Tottenham in January 2015 and Oliver Glasner versus Burnley in February 2024.

title: Sutton's predictions: Man City v Fulham - Yahoo Sports
content: The wheels have come off for Enzo Maresca at Manchester City with three Premier League defeats in a row. It's not just City's results which have been alarming, either - they were well beaten by Nottingham Forest last time out, and their performance would have been the biggest concern for their manager. In contrast, Fulham's results have improved of late and they are unbeaten in four league games. They've done all right whenever I've seen them this season, so I'm not surprised to see them picking up points. Still, the international break probably came at a good time for Maresca to sort things out. Erling Haaland is scoring again too - not that he ever really stopped for very long - and I'm expecting City to be much better here. I'm even going for them to keep a clean sheet for the first time in eight games. I'm always brave... which is why I am bottom of the predictions table.

title: Sutton's predictions: Newcastle v Arsenal - Yahoo Sports
content: I am covering this game and I think it is a huge one for Newcastle United boss Matthias Jaissle. The Magpies have picked up 12 points in their first 10 games, as they did when Eddie Howe was in charge last season, but I still don't think their fans are overly convinced by him. Some of their unease is because Newcastle don't seem to have a defined style of play and they can be a bit kamikaze going forward. Because of that, I just think Arsenal will pick them off and win comfortably. The Gunners have conceded only five league goals so far this season and they have made an incredible start to their title defence with nine wins out of 10. The worry for their rivals is that it feels to me Mikel Arteta's side haven't even got going yet, but I still don't see anyone being close to them.

title: Sutton's predictions: Tottenham v Ipswich - Yahoo Sports
content: We have seen Crystal Palace change their manager after making a disastrous start, but they are still only four points below Ipswich Town - and they will certainly see that as retrievable. The Tractor Boys are not in the relegation zone, but they are still in a relegation fight, so it is important for them to keep picking points up here and there. The trouble for them is that I don't see them getting anything at Tottenham. Spurs lost to Leeds United last time out but I still think they have turned a corner with their performances before that defeat. I actually think this will be a routine win for Roberto de Zerbi's side, and I'm going for them to keep a clean sheet too.

title: Sutton's predictions: Coventry v Crystal Palace - Yahoo Sports
content: This is the battle of the Franks... Lampard v Thomas. Thomas Frank's first conundrum as Crystal Palace's new manager is to stop them leaking so many goals. They have conceded 24 in their first 10 games, which is concerning. I still think Palace have got some really good players like Ismaila Sarr, Jorgen Strand Larsen and Jean-Philippe Mateta, so it is just a case of them getting fit and finding some form. The way Coventry play, the Eagles are going to get some chances - but can they take them? Frank Lampard's side counter-attack with such vigour, so I definitely think they will score, but I can see Palace's forward players having some joy too.

title: Sutton's predictions: Chelsea v Leeds - Yahoo Sports
content: Chelsea were so lethargic when I watched them lose against Sunderland, and I don't think they were hard done by in that game - they looked flimsy at the back, and were deservedly beaten. I had a bit of a pile-on from some Chelsea fans for saying that after the game, but then Xabi Alonso came out and was also heavily critical of the way they had defended - so he and I are on the same page there. If Joao Pedro is fit then they will at least have more physicality up front this week, but I still have a feeling Leeds will get something out of this. Daniel Farke's side got a great win over Tottenham last time out and they do not give much away - Arsenal and Brighton are the only top-flight teams to have conceded fewer league goals this season. Leeds have definitely benefited from signing keeper James Trafford, and what a move it has been for him personally as well. I admire him for that, because he could have hung around at Manchester City as Gianluigi Donnarumma's number two, but he wanted first-team football. Now he is battling it out with Jordan Pickford to be England's number one.

title: Sutton's predictions: Bournemouth v Nottingham Forest - Yahoo Sports
content: Bournemouth have won eight games in a row and it is incredible how Marco Rose has turned things around after a slow start. The Cherries were absolutely flying before the international break - but will the two weeks off affect their momentum? Forest did not need the break either, after their brilliant win over Manchester City. That was such an important result for their manager Oliver Glasner but I think they will find it difficult to follow it up at Bournemouth.

title: Sutton's predictions: Aston Villa v Sunderland - Yahoo Sports
content: I was at Sunderland's win over Chelsea and they thoroughly deserved it. They had been on a dreadful run of results before then, but it was a reminder of what they are about. Brian Brobbey was just phenomenal for the Black Cats in that game but, like his captain Granit Xhaka, he is injured and will miss out here. That just makes me think Aston Villa will have the edge. I always fancy them at home anyway with the way they go after teams, although I don't think this will be easy for them. Villa boss Unai Emery was fuming after his side threw away a two-goal lead twice in their 4-4 draw at Manchester United, but they will hold on this time while Sunderland go down fighting.

title: Hibernian v Dundee Utd: Team news - Yahoo Sports
content: Hibs welcome back Jacob Devaney and Jordan Obita after injury, but Nathan Lowe (foot), Kanayo Megwa (thigh) and Rocky Bushiri (Achilles) remain sidelined. Dundee United midfielder Emmanuel Agyei could return after a knee injury, but Neil Farrugia (groin) and Will Ferry (knee) are still out.

title: Kilmarnock v Aberdeen: Team news - Yahoo Sports
content: Kilmarnock manager Neil McCann reported a fully-fit squad apart from long-term absentee Max Stryjek (knee). Bailey Rice was back on the bench last time out and Mark O'Hara and Johnly Yfeko are pushing for recalls. But Mats Knoester, Emmanuel Gyamfi (both thigh), Kristers Tobers (knee), Chris Cadden (hamstring), Lewis Mayo (foot) and Connor Ronan (knee) are likely to remain sidelined.

title: Dundee v Hearts: Team news - Yahoo Sports
content: Dundee are still without long-term absentees Bobby Wales (ankle), Simon Murray, Finlay Robertson and Jack Moorhouse (all ACL), but Steven Pressley expects everyone else to be available. title: Celtic v St Mirren: Team news - Yahoo Sports
content: Auston Trusty is back for Celtic after a family bereavement, but Mika Baur faces 10 weeks out with an ankle injury and Alistair Johnston (hamstring) is yet to return.
