title: 3 snap count takeaways from Colts' Week 11 game v. Texans - Yahoo Sports
content: As we continue to take a look back at the Indianapolis Colts' Week 11 performance against the Houston Texans, let's highlight some noteworthy snap count figures. For the most part, when it comes to playing time, there aren't many huge surprises, but each week, there are a few things we can glean. With help from PFF, here are a few quick notes from the Colts' snap count totals from Week 11. As the Colts continue to navigate a depleted wide receiver room following the trade deadline, the team again leaned heavily on Laquon Treadwell, who played 40 of the 50 offensive snaps. Deion Burks played the second-most receiver snaps with 32, while Anthony Gould played 29. Gould led the team in slot snaps and Burks mostly lined up outside. Ashton Dulin was on the field for 22 snaps, and the combination of Quez Watkins and Nick Westbrook-Ikhine played a total of seven snaps. The Colts were without their two starting offensive tackles in this game. So, as they did last week, Matt Goncalves moved from right guard to right tackle, with Dalton Tucker taking over at right guard. Luke Tenuta then started at left tackle. Daniel Jones was under pressure on nearly 60% of his dropbacks in this game. Sauce Gardner (calf) and Charvarius Ward (knee) were both sidelined for this game. So at outside cornerback we saw Justin Walley play 61 defensive snaps. Kenneth Harris (27) and Johnathan Edwards (34) shared the workload on the opposite side. Kapena Gushiken then lined up at the nickel with Walley outside. This article originally appeared on Colts Wire: 3 snap count takeaways from Colts' Week 11 game v. Texans

title: Gasperini's press conference before Parma v Roma - AS Roma
content:
Are Mile Svilar, Gianluca Mancini and Paulo Dybala fit enough to start the game? “I think so. They've all recovered. They all stayed here and have trained well, so they're fit again. The only ones still out are [Lorenzo] Pellegrini, who we don't expect to have back in the immediate future, and [Devyne] Rensch, who has started training again at a decent intensity so could be available soon.” How would you assess these last six months, since your last meeting with Parma? “That match against Parma was a key moment because the late comeback took us from defeat to victory and paved the way for us to qualify for the Champions League – which until then we had been chasing but we weren't quite there. It was a crucial step towards the Champions League. This season is different. We've started it in a similar way to how we finished last season. Our objectives are taking shape but it's a different season. Last time we were at the end, in the last few games; now we're at the start." Have you spoken to the owners about what can be done in the transfer market? “There haven't been any such meetings for now. I think as far as transfers are concerned, it's only right that our chief executive should speak about it first. He's the one who might be able to comment on what Roma can or can't do in the January transfer window, which is always a difficult time to do business.” Matias Soule was on the bench against Como after the last international break. Will it be the same again against Parma? “It's a similar situation for the other lads who came back yesterday morning: they've trained a little bit but obviously there's the journey and the jet leg to consider. We'll have a look in training this afternoon – though it's already the last session before the match – and see how well they've recovered. That also goes for [Leonardo] Balerdi and [Santiago] Castro, who played less than the others. Soule was in superb form when he left. We have a match on Saturday, we're getting people fit again and then we have another important game on Wednesday. Then another one on Saturday and the Sunday after. Soule is definitely not a problem. The main thing is there are no injuries.” Could this be the right period for Roma to pull away in the table? “I think the season is much longer than this short period we have now. Every period is important but it can never be decisive. What's important is we stay where we are and maintain this pace.” How is Dybala exactly? He's recovered but hasn't played for a month. “We'll have to see how he gets on when he plays. Before his injury he had been training well and was playing games. It's been a month now but sooner or later he needs to start playing again. We'll assess things during the game and see how he responds. He's recovered physically – he has no problems in that sense. We'll see how his fitness is as we go.” Now that Dybala is back and Soule is in his element on the right, how do you plan to use them together? “It's not a problem whatsoever. Having them both available is a good thing – we had them both for a few weeks before Dybala got injured. Soule is performing at a very high level at the moment. I think he did well for Argentina too. He was called up to the Argentina squad, which didn't happen before. So he's made progress there. The same goes for [Rodrigo] Mora: he got called up by Portugal. I think these players are growing together and my main concern is to have them available. Getting them to play together is a non-problem. I think Dybala and Soule can play together perfectly well.” Before the international break, Roma did well in a hectic run of games despite missing players. Would you say that is a quality your team possesses? “Clearly we had other players who performed well, so we noticed the important players missing less. Now we have to push forward. We can't be looking at the past. There are always a few question marks when you start again after the break, and we need to get rid of them as quickly as we can. We hope to pick up from where we left off, against Sassuolo, but we can't be sure about what shape all the players are in. That's the main problem when you have an international break. First there were three weeks and now another two weeks, not far apart from each other. And they play different amounts. [Evan] Ndicka played two games while others got no minutes at all. It very much depends on the individual. It's mainly the first game back when you have that uncertainty. We're looking to continue our run of results, and our performances. We have to hit the ground running again, in Parma, which is anything but an easy game. The league table is starting to take shape at both ends and teams are becoming more determined to pick up points, as they're becoming more and more important”. “Gila did very well at Genoa, taking a team in Serie B and winning the league to get them back up to Serie A. He's always done well and has had some difficulties results-wise at some clubs, but his teams are always difficult to play against – they're very compact and well organised. It will be the same again this time. Two games ago he beat Atalanta 3-0 in Bergamo, then he lost to Bologna last time out, but they were reduced to ten men early on. I'm very wary of him and Parma. I know what Serie A is like and these games are your proverbial banana skins, especially after the international break when we're not exactly sure where we stand. That's why this is a very important game.” At the end of the summer window you said that your squad was a little short numbers-wise. Do you expect to address that in January? “It's the 20th November so any assessments we make now mean very little. Every club, including Roma, is looking around, but I don't think anything can be determined now for anyone. There are lots of games still to play and anything can happen: players who aren't playing now can start playing and do really well, and vice versa. Right now my sole focus is on the league. Obviously I'm in constant contact with [Tony] D'Amico but as far as transfers go nothing has been planned yet, other than what's been said between me and D'Amico.” Including last season, after the international breaks Roma have won one, lost three and drawn one. Is that just a coincidence? “I hope so! Those numbers make for uncomfortable reading. We have to balance it out a bit better!” “That was the final step he needed to take to get back to his former self because he's always had a superb strike on him. It's always been a key part of his game. Hopefully he can get back to taking set-pieces the way he used to – those free kicks. We're missing a few set-piece goals. That was something he was really good at.” “I think our organisation, our approach to games and our shape are all better than they were last season. That's important. There are an infinite number of ways in which you can improve. Obviously you work on the small details, which are often decisive. Small details are the difference between scoring or not scoring, conceding or not conceding. When you have an established set-up that all the players identify with, those small details make the difference.” © 2018-2026 A.S. Roma S.r.l. – EU VAT IT01180281006 - all rights reserved. title: Best Used Honda CR-V Years to Buy (and the Model Years to Avoid) - MotorTrend
content: The CR-V has earned its sterling reputation, but some model years are smarter buys than others. The Honda CR-V is a cornerstone of the American car market, often trading bestselling SUV accolades with its closest rival, the Toyota RAV4. If you’re considering one, you’ve considered the other, and you’re almost certainly here because you’ve landed on the Honda. As much as it’s done to earn its sterling reputation over the past 30 years, though, not every single one is a smart buy. It’s a good rule of thumb with any car purchase to take a wait-and-see approach when a new-generation vehicle is launched. Automakers spend years putting millions of miles on test vehicles before new models are released, but still, problems can emerge later that didn’t show up in testing. CR-Vs, as good as they are historically, compared to the other compact SUVs in its class, are not immune to this. According to research by extended warranty provider CoverageX (which is very motivated to know which used cars it should or shouldn’t give extended warranties to), the CR-V fits this pattern of notable issues occurring with its new-generation model launches. Its research goes back to 2007, which saw the birth of the third-generation CR-V. For that and each successive generation (not including the too-new-for-data sixth generation), there’s a serious mechanical issue to be on the lookout for. In each case, the issue is resolved within two to three years, so if you’re looking at a CR-V from the earlier part of its generation, make sure those issues have been professionally repaired. Early third-generation CR-Vs from the 2007 to 2009 model years have a known issue with the air conditioning compressor, potentially causing it to fail in fewer than 90,000 miles. You’ll be hard-pressed to find a CR-V that old with so few miles on it, so there’s a good chance the compressor has already been replaced, but it never hurts to check the paperwork. The 2010 and 2011 models have upgraded compressors, though on those models, you’ll still want to listen for a rattling timing chain on cold starts that may need work. Similarly, early fourth-generation CR-Vs have their own quirks. The 2012 to 2014 model years are known to wear out their engine mounts in fewer than 110,000 miles. Here, again, they’ll likely have been replaced by now, but you should still ask. The most serious CR-V issue affects early fifth-generation models, including the 2017, 2018, and 2019 model years equipped with the 1.5-liter turbocharged four-cylinder engine, which suffered from oil dilution, particularly in cold climates. On cold engine starts, gasoline can seep past the piston rings and into the crankcase, diluting the oil and reducing its lubricating properties. Left untreated, it can lead to sludge in the oil and engine damage where things aren’t properly lubricated. The 2020 and 2021 CR-Vs received updated software to improve cold starting, which reduced the incidence of problems, and by the 2022 model year it had been fixed. Those same early fifth-generation years (2017 to 2019) are also known for a shuddering in the continuously variable automatic transmission (CVT) under acceleration. It’s a less common problem and often fixed by changing the transmission fluid, but it’s worth keeping an eye out for. Generally, the older a car, the less safe it is compared to a newer version. All those airbags and electronic control gizmos do add weight, cost, and complexity to modern cars, but they also keep us exponentially safer than in the past in the event of a crash. All Honda CR-Vs have come equipped with front, side, and side curtain airbags (at a minimum), as well as stability and traction control since 2005. Prior to that, it was just front airbags and traction control. Honda introduced its signature ACE body structure in the CR-V in 2007 with the third-generation SUV, greatly improving its front crash protection. For the fourth-generation model in 2012, Honda tied the all-wheel-drive system and the stability control system together for the first time, enhancing the stability control computer’s ability to correct a skid. Later, during a 2015 midcycle update, Honda introduced its Honda Sensing suite of active and passive safety aids to the top trim CR-V Touring. Honda Sensing would become standard on all CR-V trim levels above LX starting in 2017 and would subsequently gain additional functions and features in intervening years. (Honda Sensing is now standard on all Honda automobiles today.) Newer cars generally get better fuel economy than the ones they replace, but the CR-V has always been relatively efficient, so it hasn’t always improved by leaps and bounds. Since the day it went on sale in 1997, the CR-V has never returned worse than 21 mpg combined. Things didn’t really take off until the third generation, however, when combined fuel economy improved by 2 mpg. The 2017 model saw another 2-mpg gain, but that jumped to a 4-mpg improvement if you got the new 1.5-liter turbo engine (which had its own issues, as we’ve discussed). The biggest improvement came in 2020 with the introduction of the CR-V Hybrid. This brought fuel economy up to 38 mpg combined, and it now sits as high as 40 mpg. Unless you’re prepared to install aftermarket equipment, the older your car, the less features it’s likely to have. Before you look at old CR-Vs, consider which features you can’t live without. For example, the first CR-V to have Bluetooth connectivity for your phone was the 2012 model. The first to get Apple CarPlay and Android Auto was the 2017 model, and wireless CarPlay and Android Auto didn’t arrive until the 2023 model, which was also the first to get a wireless phone charger. Then there are the more basic features. The CR-V didn’t get a power driver’s seat until 2008, the same year it got dual-zone climate control for the first time. The 60/40 split-folding rear seat didn’t become standard equipment until 2012. 2010–2011: Late third-generation cars have the air conditioning problem ironed out, plus the benefit of the updated body structure for better crash protection. 2015–2016: The refreshed fourth-generation models are a high point in CR-V history, with no major problems, good fuel economy, and modern crash avoidance technologies. 2022–2026: The last year of the fifth generation had all its problems resolved, CarPlay and Android Auto built-in, and a hybrid model with excellent fuel economy. The sixth-generation cars (starting in 2023) have only improved upon the 2022 model with even better fuel economy, wireless CarPlay and Android Auto, and the most up-to-date safety equipment. 2007–2009: A bad A/C compressor is an expensive fix, so if you’re looking at these model years, make sure it’s already been professionally replaced. 2012–2014: Cracked engine mounts can lead to bigger problems, so make sure they’ve been inspected or replaced if you’re shopping these years. 2017–2019: Oil dilution can, if left untreated long enough, lead to engine failure, so make sure any car from these years—especially one suspected of having made short trips in cold weather—has had all its software updates and regular oil changes before you buy. Were you one of those kids who taught themselves to identify cars at night by their headlights and taillights? I was. I was also one of those kids with a huge box of Hot Wheels and impressive collection of home-made Lego hot rods. I asked my parents for a Power Wheels Porsche 911 for Christmas for years, though the best I got was a pedal-powered tractor. I drove the wheels off it. I used to tell my friends I’d own a “slug bug” one day. When I was 15, my dad told me he would get me a car on the condition that I had to maintain it. He came back with a rough-around-the-edges 1967 Volkswagen Beetle he’d picked up for something like $600. I drove the wheels off that thing, too, even though it was only slightly faster than the tractor. When I got tired of chasing electrical gremlins (none of which were related to my bitchin’ self-installed stereo, thank you very much), I thought I’d move on to something more sensible. I bought a 1986 Pontiac Fiero GT and got my first speeding ticket in that car during the test drive. Not my first-ever ticket, mind you. That came behind the wheel of a Geo Metro hatchback I delivered pizza in during high school. I never planned to have this job. I was actually an aerospace engineering major in college, but calculus and I had a bad breakup. Considering how much better my English grades were than my calculus grades, I decided to stick to my strengths and write instead. When I made the switch, people kept asking me what I wanted to do with my life. I told them I’d like to write for a car magazine someday, not expecting it to actually happen. I figured I’d be in newspapers, maybe a magazine if I was lucky. Then this happened, which was slightly awkward because I grew up reading Car & Driver, but convenient since I don’t live in Michigan. Now I just try to make it through the day without adding any more names to the list of people who want to kill me and take my job.
